an0809.user: Running our logistics SaaS acquisition mostly through email-led campaigns. Last 30 days: AOV ₹2,400, gross margin 49%, CAC ₹580, ROAS 4.1, CTR 2.5%. On paper this looks healthy and I'm tempted to pour more budget in. But I'm new to reading these — what's the non-obvious thing I'm missing here?
an0809.assistant:
Your first-order economics are genuinely good: ₹2,400 × 49% − ₹580 = +₹596 contribution per order, and 4.1 ROAS confirms acquisition is working. So the surface read is right — nothing wrong at the top.

The leak is downstream. Your 90-day repeat is 11%. That means roughly 9 in 10 customers buy once and never come back. For a SaaS that should be a recurring-revenue business, a single-order LTV is the whole problem — your model only works if people stick. Right now you're acquiring efficiently and then quietly losing almost everyone.

That changes what you do next. Pouring more spend in just fills a bucket with no bottom faster — you'll book more first orders and the same 89% will churn. Fix retention before you scale: onboarding, the second-month activation moment, why month-2 logins drop. Get repeat from 11% toward something defensible, then the acquisition engine you've already built becomes worth feeding.

One caveat — 30 days is short to read 90-day repeat cleanly; pull the actual cohort curve by signup month to confirm the drop-off point before you act. But the direction is clear: retention, not budget, is your lever.

an0810.user: Okay I'm a bit stressed about this. Flipkart seller, scaling our Google Search spend hard. Eight weeks ago I was at ₹3L/month, CAC ₹612, ROAS 3.2. Now I'm at ₹6.3L, CAC has climbed to ₹863 and ROAS dropped to 2.3. AOV ₹1,950, margin 64%. Did Google's algorithm change on me? Why is everything getting worse as I spend more??
an0810.assistant:
Breathe — nothing broke. This is exactly what a working channel looks like when you push past its efficient size. You doubled spend (₹3L → ₹6.3L), and CAC went ₹612 → ₹863 while ROAS slid 3.2 → 2.3. That's not the algorithm turning on you; that's saturation.

Here's the mechanism. Your first ₹3L was buying the highest-intent searchers — the people already typing exactly what you sell. There's a finite pool of those. To spend the next ₹3.3L, Google had to reach colder, broader, lower-intent queries, and colder traffic costs more to convert. The rising CAC IS the signal that you've drained the cheap intent and are now paying up for the marginal buyer.

The economics still hold — ₹1,950 × 64% − ₹863 = +₹385 per order, so you're not bleeding. But your efficient ceiling on this channel is real, and more budget into the same finite pool just keeps dragging the average up.

The lever isn't budget, it's new demand: fresh audiences, new keyword clusters, a second channel. Expand the pool before you expand the spend. One check first — confirm CAC is rising on stable conversion volume and not a seasonal dip in Flipkart search; pull the weekly trend to be sure.

an0811.user: Vertical SaaS for clinics, running YouTube. Pasting last 8 weeks: spend went ₹3.5L → ₹7.6L, CAC ₹622 → ₹876, ROAS 3.5 → 2.5, AOV ₹2,150, margin 56%. What's wrong?
an0811.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with the channel — you've simply found its ceiling. You more than doubled spend (₹3.5L → ₹7.6L) and the numbers moved exactly the way a saturating channel moves: CAC ₹622 → ₹876, ROAS 3.5 → 2.5.

The why: your early budget mopped up the clinics with the strongest fit — the ones YouTube could match cheaply. That audience is finite. To absorb an extra ₹4.1L, the platform had to serve colder, less-qualified viewers, and cold reach converts worse, so each new customer costs more. The climbing CAC isn't waste — it's the price of the marginal, lower-intent buyer.

The unit economics are still positive: ₹2,150 × 56% − ₹876 = +₹328 per order. So don't cut. But realise that adding budget to the same audience pool just keeps pushing CAC up the curve.

Your lever is new demand, not more spend: new creative angles for a different clinic segment, new targeting, or a second channel to open a fresh pool. One caveat — 8 weeks of aggressive scaling can blur with creative wear; check whether frequency and CTR also slipped, because that would mean fatigue is stacked on top of saturation.

an0812.user: Small D2C candle brand testing YouTube. In the last 7 days I spent ₹18K and got 11 conversions. Is my CAC good? Should I scale this or kill it?
an0812.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't know yet, and neither can I. 11 conversions over 7 days is far too small to conclude anything — whatever CAC or ROAS you compute off it is statistical noise, not a real read. One good day or one dud day swings the whole number.

So don't scale and don't kill on this. Both are guesses dressed up as decisions.

Let it run until you have roughly 100 conversions, or a clean 2–3 week window — whichever comes first. That's the point where the CAC stabilises enough to actually trust. Until you cross that threshold, the only mistake available is reacting to a number that hasn't formed yet. Keep the budget steady, leave the creative alone, and check back when the sample is real.

an0813.user: D2C apparel label, acquiring through email. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,250, margin 32%, CAC ₹748, ROAS 1.7, CTR 1.7%. My CAC feels too high for the category. How do I bring my CAC down?
an0813.assistant:
You're aiming at the wrong target. Run the contribution: ₹1,250 × 32% − ₹748 = −₹348 per order. You lose money on every sale, and no CAC tweak closes a ₹348 hole.

Look at why. Even if a brilliant campaign cut CAC to a category-leading ₹500, you'd still make ₹400 − ₹500 = −₹100 per order. The math only turns positive once gross margin clears ₹748 per order, which at ₹1,250 AOV means a margin near 60%. You're at 32%. That's not a marketing number — that's COGS, pricing, and discounting.

So this is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. The CAC isn't even outrageous; it's just heavier than a thin-margin product can carry. Chasing lower CAC here is treating a symptom.

The lever is the P&L, not the ad account: raise prices, cut COGS, or lift AOV (bundles, higher-value SKUs) until each order actually has enough margin to pay for its own acquisition. Caveat — confirm 32% is true gross margin after returns and shipping, not a blended estimate; if returns are eating it, that's the first place to dig.

This isn't a CAC problem. It's a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Your 2.4% CTR is actually healthy — the front of the funnel is doing its job; the back-end economics just can't pay it back.

Fix the P&L first: negotiate COGS, raise price, or push AOV up with bundles so there's enough margin to fund acquisition at all. an0819.user: Test-prep edtech, running Meta. Last 30 days: 1.26M impressions, 21,896 clicks, CTR 1.7%, 93 orders, conversion rate 0.42%, AOV ₹850. Targeting is broad / interest-based. Why is my CTR low?

The mechanism is in the line you mentioned last: broad / interest-based targeting. You're paying for a flood of clicks from people who are curious, not committed — students browsing, parents window-shopping, the broadly-interested. So the fix isn't a punchier ad to lift CTR — it'd just buy more low-intent clicks. The lever is tightening intent: move from broad interests to high-intent signals — people actively searching for your exam, lookalikes off actual purchasers, retargeting pools — and stop optimising the campaign for link clicks; optimise for purchases so Meta hunts buyers, not browsers. an0820.user: D2C apparel, Google Search heavy. Post-iOS this is doing my head in. Meta's dashboard says 3.7 ROAS, my Shopify last-click says 1.9, on ₹9.5L spend this month. The two numbers won't agree and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. What's wrong?
an0820.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with your account — you're stuck refereeing two dashboards that are structurally built to disagree, and neither is 'the truth'.

Here's why they diverge. The platform's 3.7 leans on modelled conversions and a 7-day-click (often plus view-through) window — it's incentivised to claim credit and will over-count. Shopify last-click at 1.9 hands all credit to the final click and gives the assist channels zero — so it under-counts anything that touched the customer earlier. Post-iOS signal loss widens the gap further. Both are biased in opposite directions; reality sits somewhere between 1.9 and 3.7. Trying to decide which dashboard is 'correct' is a question with no answer.

Stop trying. The lever is to anchor on a number neither platform can spin: blended CAC = total spend ÷ actual new customers. Take your ₹9.5L, divide by the count of genuinely new customers Shopify recorded this month, and manage the whole business to that single figure over time. It doesn't care whose pixel fired — it's just cash in versus customers out.

Caveat — 'new customers' has to mean first-time buyers, not all orders, or you'll flatter yourself. Clean that definition, watch blended CAC trend month over month, and let the two ROAS numbers argue in the corner.

an0822.user: IELTS edtech, Amazon Ads. This week vs last week my ROAS dropped about 15%. We had 109 conversions this week. I'm pretty sophisticated about this stuff and I'm ready to overhaul the entire strategy this weekend — before I do, sanity check me?
an0822.assistant:
Sanity check: don't touch anything. A 15% ROAS move week-over-week on 109 conversions is well inside normal variance — it's noise, not a trend. At that sample size, the random week-to-week wobble alone can swing ROAS more than 15% in either direction without a single thing actually changing in your account.

Overhauling strategy off one noisy week is how good operators whipsaw their own accounts: you tear up a working setup, the next week reverts to the mean anyway, and now you can't tell what your changes did. You'd be adding chaos, not signal.

So this weekend, do nothing. A real shift looks like one of two things: the same direction sustained for 3–4 consecutive weeks, or a single move large enough to clearly clear the noise band — a drop more like 35–40% on stable volume, not 15%. Until you see that, this is just the metric breathing.

Mark the line in the sand now — 'I act only if it's down 3+ weeks running or down >35% on this volume' — so next week's number can't bait you into a reaction you'll regret.
